overview.text: Addition, also called adding or summation, is the operation that combines two or more quantities into a sum; the quantities are addends (or summands), and repeated addition can be written with capital sigma notation. For ordinary numbers, changing the order or grouping of addends does not change the sum, and adding zero leaves a number unchanged. The same idea extends beyond numbers, but the objects must follow rules for their type: vector addition combines directed movements into a resultant, drawable by placing arrows tip-to-tail, while matrix addition adds matching entries and requires matrices of identical dimensions. These extensions make addition useful for describing combined quantities, displacements, and data arrays.

key_facts.text: The result of addition is a sum; the quantities being added are called addends or summands.
For real numbers, addition is commutative (a + b = b + a) and associative ((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)).
Zero is the additive identity for real numbers: adding zero leaves a number unchanged.
To draw a vector sum, place the second vector’s starting point at the first vector’s arrowhead; the resultant runs from the first vector’s start to the second’s end.
Matrix addition pairs corresponding entries, so the matrices must have the same dimensions; the resulting matrix keeps those dimensions.
Repeated addition can be represented using capital sigma notation, with limits indicating the terms included in the sum.
